entries.concept: Form 8-K current report (material corporate events)
questions: did apple file an 8-K this week
any material events at tesla lately
what has X disclosed since its last 10-Q
what did X tell the SEC recently
entries.market_reading: The investor wants the discrete corporate events the company was obliged to report between periodic reports, and which of them are bad news. The item code classifies the event. A small set of items is read as negative on its face (1.03 bankruptcy, 2.04 debt acceleration, 2.06 material impairment, 3.01 listing deficiency, 4.02 non-reliance, 1.05 material cyber incident, 4.01 when the auditor resigned or there were disagreements, 5.02 unplanned departures of the CEO/CFO or a director quitting over a disagreement); most other items are neutral until read.

entries.formula: List the 8-K and 8-K/A filings in a window, group them by item code, and classify each item using the family notes table (negative on its face / depends on content / neutral).
entries.period_convention: Since the latest 10-K or 10-Q, or the trailing 12 months. Date each event by its event date, not the filing date; the filing is normally due four business days after the event.
entries.frame_notes: For an event, 'absolute' means the filing itself is the signal (the question 'did X report a ...' is answered yes or no); 'history' means first occurrence versus repetition within the company's own recent record; 'peers' means how common the event is among companies of the same filer status or size, which is the only honest way to call one company's record unusual. Nothing makes a company's 8-K count 'high' or 'low': a large company files many routine 8-Ks. Judge items, not volume.
entries.direction: depends on the item (see the item entries RF-02 to RF-30)

thresholds.line: filed or furnished within four business days after the event unless the item says otherwise
thresholds.meaning: the filing deadline; a late 8-K is itself a compliance lapse

thresholds.line: no 10b-5 liability solely for failing to file Items 1.01, 1.02, 1.05, 2.03, 2.04, 2.05, 2.06, 4.02(a), 5.02(e), 6.03
thresholds.meaning: the safe-harbour items: the safe harbour covers only the failure to file the 8-K, and only until the due date of the periodic report for the period, which must then carry the disclosure. It does not permit silence, and an absent 8-K for these items reads cannot establish.

entries.concept: Form 8-K Item 1.01 Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement
questions: did X sign a big contract
did nvidia sign a merger agreement
has X entered a material deal
any major supply deal for X
entries.market_reading: The investor wants to know whether the company signed (or materially amended) an agreement outside the ordinary course that binds it to material obligations: merger agreements, credit facilities, large supply or licence deals, financing commitments. It is not negative by itself; the terms decide it (dilutive financing, change-of-control clauses, parties related to insiders).

questions: did X lose a major contract
was the merger with X terminated
did the deal fall through for X
did X's credit line get terminated
entries.market_reading: The investor wants to know whether a material agreement ended early (not by expiry or completion). entries.concept: Bankruptcy or receivership (Form 8-K Item 1.03)
questions: is my stock worthless after chapter 11
did bed bath and beyond file for bankruptcy
what happens to shareholders if X goes bankrupt
entries.market_reading: The investor wants to know whether the company (or its parent) is in a bankruptcy or receivership proceeding, and what that means for the shares. It is the most negative event for common shareholders: in a reorganisation, equity is last in line, and a plan crammed down over a dissenting senior class cannot leave anything to a junior class, so old shares are frequently cancelled or heavily diluted.

figures.unit: event (filing date; event date stated in the body)
figures.notes: The trigger date is the event date; the filing is due within four business days unless the item says otherwise. 1.03(b) covers the later confirmation of a plan of reorganisation or liquidation. | element notes: EDGAR submission metadata 'items' field (filer-declared item codes) ; item headings in the 8-K body text

figures.notes: element notes: 10-K Item 3 / 10-Q Part II Item 1

entries.formula: Flag Item 1.03 filings and show each with its event date, its age and its sub-item: 1.03(a), a receiver or similar officer appointed or a court assuming jurisdiction, for the registrant or its parent; 1.03(b), an order confirming a plan, which is often an emergence, not a new bankruptcy. An old 1.03 never supports 'is bankrupt' now, and the line quotes the item title (review R7). No computation.
entries.period_convention: Event date = date the court or authority assumed jurisdiction (petition date).
entries.frame_notes: Absolute: the filing is the answer. Earlier warning signs belong to other entries (going concern RF-33, debt acceleration RF-10, late filings RF-31, delisting notices RF-13).

thresholds.line: 11 USC 1129(b)(2)(B): a plan confirmed over an impaired class of unsecured claims that has not accepted it must give each holder property worth, as of the plan's effective date, the allowed amount of the claim ((B)(i)), or else no holder of a junior claim or interest, including the common equity, may receive or retain any property on account of it ((B)(ii)). (C) applies the same rule to a dissenting class of interests, such as preferred stock, protecting it only against interests junior to it. Common stock has no class junior to it, so (C) gives it no protection.
thresholds.meaning: why common equity usually recovers little or nothing in a contested Chapter 11: unless every dissenting senior unsecured class is paid the full allowed amount of its claims, old equity cannot retain anything on account of its shares (1129(b)(2)(B)(ii)).

did X's auditor give an adverse opinion on controls
has X fixed its material weakness
entries.market_reading: The investor wants to know whether management (and, for larger filers, the auditor) concluded that internal control over financial reporting is not effective because of at least one material weakness, what it is, and whether it has persisted. A material weakness means a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be caught in time; it is read as a red flag and often accompanies restatements. How unusual it is depends heavily on company size.

entries.concept: Going-concern doubt (auditor's paragraph under PCAOB AS 2415; management's disclosure under ASC 205-40)
aka: ability to continue as a going concern
questions: does X have a going concern warning
is there substantial doubt about X surviving
will X run out of money
did X's auditor flag going concern
is X at risk of failing within a year
entries.market_reading: The investor wants to know whether the auditor (in the audit report) or management (in the notes) has raised substantial doubt that the company can continue operating for about the next year. It is one of the strongest distress signals in a filing and is read as negative, though its absence gives no assurance.

figures.name: Auditor's going-concern explanatory paragraph
figures.notes: In the audit report, which is not XBRL-tagged; the paragraph must use the terms 'substantial doubt' and 'going concern'.

figures.name: Management's going-concern disclosure
figures.notes: Element names checked in the 2026 us-gaap schema (S77); use depends on the filer. SubstantialDoubtAboutGoingConcernTextBlock and ...ConditionsOrEvents are also used when doubt was alleviated. On their own they do not establish unalleviated doubt. Read the filing text, the NotAlleviated element or WithinOneYear before stating 'substantial doubt'.

figures.name: Management's disclosure: substantial doubt raised, alleviated by management's plans
figures.notes: Never supports a 'substantial doubt exists' reading. Case shows it as 'doubt raised, alleviated by plans'.

entries.formula: Read us-gaap:SubstantialDoubtAboutGoingConcernWithinOneYear first. true supports, unless the same filing tags us-gaap:SubstantialDoubtAboutGoingConcernManagementsPlansSubstantialDoubtAlleviated; false argues against the management path. A tagged us-gaap:SubstantialDoubtAboutGoingConcernManagementsPlansSubstantialDoubtNotAlleviated supports. Doubt that was raised and then alleviated by management's plans is a disclosed condition. It is not a going-concern finding: show it and label it 'alleviated'. The text path supports only from the notes to the financial statements, and never on negated, alleviated, conditional or risk-factor wording. The auditor's explanatory paragraph under PCAOB AS 2415 supports on its own, whatever management tagged. No tag and no text reads cannot establish, never 'no doubt'. No computation.
entries.period_convention: Each annual audit report; management also evaluates at each interim period.
entries.frame_notes: For an event, 'absolute' means the filing itself is the signal (the question 'did X report a ...' is answered yes or no); 'history' means first occurrence versus repetition within the company's own recent record; 'peers' means how common the event is among companies of the same filer status or size, which is the only honest way to call one company's record unusual. History = consecutive years with the paragraph (many micro-caps carry it for years).

thresholds.meaning: PCAOB's horizon for the auditor's evaluation (AS 2415 .02), applied by the auditor. It runs from the date of the audited statements and is a going-concern horizon, not a line for 'enough cash'

thresholds.meaning: FASB's going-concern window for management (ASC 205-40, by reference), which can end later than the auditor's; a horizon, not a line for 'enough cash'

entries.concept: Legal proceedings, loss contingencies and regulatory investigations (Reg S-K Item 103; ASC 450-20)
questions: how much could X lose in litigation
entries.market_reading: The investor wants to know what material litigation or government proceedings the company faces, how much it has accrued, and the reasonably possible loss beyond that. Read as negative in proportion to the exposure relative to the company's size; government investigations and securities class actions after a restatement or stock drop are read as red flags.

figures.notes: The difference between the maximum estimated loss and the amount recorded at the balance-sheet date. LossContingencyRangeOfPossibleLossMaximum/Minimum are absent from the 2026 schema; older filings may use them.

figures.notes: LitigationSettlementAmountAwardedToOtherParty is the amount awarded in a judgment or settlement, read as a magnitude; its schema balance is credit, so do not add it to expense lines without flipping the sign. LossContingencyLossInPeriod is the accrual charge (debit), which can be negative when a loss is reversed. GainLossRelatedToLitigationSettlement is credit-balanced (positive = gain) and also covers insurance claims, so it is not used here. Balances from the 2026 schema (S77).

Estimate of possible loss (shown beside the exposure, never added)

does X exclude stock comp from earnings
gap between GAAP and adjusted earnings at X
entries.market_reading: The investor wants to know how far the company's own 'adjusted' profit departs from GAAP profit, whether the gap is growing, and whether excluded items (restructuring, impairments, stock compensation, 'one-time' costs) actually recur. A large or widening gap, recurring 'non-recurring' items, or adjustments that remove normal cash operating costs are read as a quality-of-earnings red flag.

entries.concept: Beneish M-score (earnings manipulation probability, Beneish 1999)
questions: does X look like an earnings manipulator
entries.market_reading: The investor wants a quantitative screen of whether the company's financial statements look like those of firms later found to have overstated earnings: receivables outgrowing sales, falling margins, rising capitalised costs, fast growth, slowing depreciation, rising SG&A, rising leverage and high accruals. A score above the paper's cut-off is read as a red flag that warrants reading the filings, not as proof.

Income from continuing operations and operating cash flow (accruals)

entries.formula: Eight year-over-year indices from two consecutive annual statements: DSRI (receivables/sales this year over last), GMI (last year's gross margin over this year's), AQI (share of assets other than current assets and PP&E, this over last), SGI (sales growth), DEPI (depreciation rate last over this), SGAI (SG&A/sales this over last), LVGI (debt/assets this over last), TATA (total accruals / total assets). M = the paper's unweighted probit: -4.840 + 0.920 DSRI + 0.528 GMI + 0.404 AQI + 0.892 SGI + 0.115 DEPI - 0.172 SGAI + 4.679 TATA - 0.327 LVGI. Probability of manipulation = standard normal CDF of M.
entries.period_convention: Latest fiscal year versus the prior fiscal year (annual data only).
entries.frame_notes: 'Absolute' = against the paper's cut-off; 'history' = the company's own M-score trend (a jump matters more than one reading).

thresholds.meaning: the paper's cut-off, chosen for relative error costs of 20:1 or 30:1; in the paper's estimation sample it misclassified 26% of manipulators and 13.8% of non-manipulators

thresholds.meaning: the paper's cut-off at a 10:1 error-cost ratio

entries.concept: Piotroski F-score (financial strength among value stocks, Piotroski 2000)
questions: is X financially strong by piotroski
does X pass the piotroski test
entries.market_reading: The investor wants a nine-point check of improving fundamentals (profitability, cash generation, leverage, liquidity, dilution, margins, turnover). A high score (8-9) marks financially strong firms; a low score (0-1) weak ones. It was designed to separate winners from losers among cheap (high book-to-market) stocks.

figures.name: Net income before extraordinary items and operating cash flow

entries.formula: Nine binary signals, each 1 if good: ROA > 0; CFO > 0; ROA higher than last year; CFO > ROA (accruals); long-term debt to average total assets fell; current ratio rose; no common equity issued in the prior year; gross margin rose; asset turnover (sales / beginning total assets) rose. ROA and CFO are scaled by beginning-of-year total assets. F = sum (0-9).
entries.period_convention: Latest fiscal year versus the prior fiscal year.
entries.frame_notes: 'Absolute' = the paper's portfolio groups (high 8-9, low 0-1); 'history' = change in the company's own score.

thresholds.line: F = 8 or 9 = 'high F_SCORE' (strong); F = 0 or 1 = 'low F_SCORE' (weak)
thresholds.meaning: the paper's portfolio classification; it is a ranking device, not a pass mark

entries.market_reading: The investor wants to know how much of reported earnings is accruals rather than cash. entries.formula: Sloan (1996): accruals = (change in current assets - change in cash) - (change in current liabilities - change in short-term debt - change in taxes payable) - depreciation, divided by average total assets. entries.concept: Dechow F-score (probability of material accounting misstatement, Dechow, Ge, Larson and Sloan 2011)
questions: is X at risk of an accounting misstatement
entries.market_reading: The investor wants a score of how closely the company's financial statements resemble those of firms the SEC later charged with material misstatement (accrual growth, receivables and inventory build-ups, soft assets, cash sales, ROA change, capital raising). The score is scaled so 1.0 equals the average firm's risk; higher is riskier. (Not to be confused with Piotroski's F-score.)

figures.name: Inputs: total assets, cash, investments, liabilities, preferred stock, receivables, inventory, net PP&E, sales, net income, issuance of debt or equity

entries.formula: Model 1 (financial statement variables only): logit = -7.893 + 0.790 RSST accruals + 2.518 change in receivables + 1.191 change in inventory + 1.979 % soft assets + 0.171 change in cash sales - 0.932 change in ROA + 1.029 issuance dummy; probability = e^logit / (1 + e^logit); F-score = probability / 0.0037 (the sample's unconditional misstatement rate).
entries.period_convention: Latest fiscal year versus prior (some inputs need two prior years).
entries.frame_notes: 'Absolute' = against 1.0 (average risk) and the paper's reference lines; 'history' = trend in the company's score.

thresholds.line: F = 1.0 means risk equal to the unconditional (average) rate; above 1 = above-average risk

entries.concept: Reverse stock splits (often to cure a listing deficiency)
aka: reverse stock split to stay listed
questions: did X do a reverse split
why did X reverse split its stock
is X reverse splitting to avoid delisting
how many reverse splits has X done
reverse stock split X nasdaq compliance
entries.market_reading: The investor wants to know whether the company combined its shares, usually to lift a sub-$1 price back above an exchange minimum. Among small companies it is read as a distress signal, and repeated reverse splits are a strong red flag; the exchanges themselves have limited compliance periods for companies that use them serially.

figures.name: Charter amendment or board action (Form 8-K Item 5.03 or 3.03) and exchange notices (3.01)
Split ratio and description
figures.notes: Fallback: the Form 8-K (Item 5.03 or 3.03) or the exchange notice that states the ratio. The ratio element's definition covers both directions ('one share converted to two or two shares converted to one') and does not fix whether a 1-for-10 is tagged 10 or 0.1; read the direction from the StockholdersEquityReverseStockSplit text or the 8-K, never from the number alone. Do not derive the ratio from two share counts: a before/after count mixes issuance and buybacks between the two dates with the split, and restated prior-period counts (e.g. weighted-average shares in a later filing) already reflect the split, so the quotient tends to 1. Keep dei:EntityCommonStockSharesOutstanding only as context, not as a ratio input.

entries.frame_notes: 'History' = number and cumulative ratio of reverse splits over two years.

notes: Source IDs (S01-S83) are family-wide: the same ID means the same source in every entry, so a builder can de-duplicate. Quotes appear only for US-government public-domain text fetched in this run (eCFR, Federal Register, uscode.house.gov) and are 25 words or fewer; the FR 'little r' quote normalises the Federal Register's typographic quote marks to plain ones. Element names: us-gaap names were checked by name against FASB's us-gaap-2026.xsd (identifiers only; no labels or documentation copied); dei/cyd/ecd names were observed in a filed 2026 10-K held as a project fixture; 8-K item codes come from EDGAR submission metadata, which the project's edgar_submissions connector already parses. The check was done directly on the schema file instead. Event entries: 'frames' use 'absolute' for 'the filing is the answer', 'history' for repetition within the company, and 'peers' for base rates by filer status; no_market_threshold=true on an event entry means no authoritative source makes the event count or size 'high' or 'low' (definitional filing rules are still listed). Negative-on-its-face 8-K items: 1.03, 1.05, 2.04, 2.06, 3.01 (except voluntary transfers), 4.02, 6.04; negative when certain facts are present: 4.01 (resignation, disagreements, reportable events), 5.02 (5.02(a) disagreement or removal for cause; unexplained CFO/CAO exits), 1.02 (loss of key contract or financing), 3.02 (large or serial dilution), 5.05 (waiver for a senior officer), 5.06/shell status; neutral until read: 1.01, 2.01, 2.02, 2.03, 2.05 (mixed), 3.03, 5.01, 5.03, 5.04, 5.07, 5.08, 7.01, 8.01, 9.01. Size matters: SEC staff data show ineffective ICFR at about 40% of non-accelerated filers but about 4% of large accelerated filers, and late 10-Ks at 28% vs 6%; for the coverage desk's small and micro-cap names a builder must compare within filer status, never across the whole market. Pending 2026 SEC proposals (semiannual reporting via Form 10-S; simplified filer status; proxy solicitation modernisation; rescission of climate rules) could change deadlines and late-filing logic if adopted; recheck before relying on the 10-Q cadence.
